common_name: Heaven's Gate Coreopsis (Bicolor Rose-Red Pink Tickseed)

planting.note: Set out container plants after last frost in consistently moist, well-drained soil; unlike drought-tough coreopsis, C. rosea cultivars need reliable moisture to perform well.

directions: Plant in medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun, watering during dry spells since Coreopsis rosea and its cultivars have far less drought tolerance than other tickseeds. Discovered as a branch mutation of the earlier cultivar 'Sweet Dreams', Heaven's Gate bears daisy-like flowers with rose-pink petals surrounding a darker rose-red ring around a golden center, deeper and more saturated in color than its parent. It is sterile and produces no viable seed, so it will not self-sow, and it spreads slowly by rhizome to form a neat mound of fine, threadlike foliage. Deadhead spent stalks to encourage continued bloom from summer into autumn.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring in moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to part shade, mimicking the open pineywoods seeps and bog margins where this rare species is found in the wild.

directions: Rudbeckia scabrifolia is a rare native limited in the wild to a handful of parishes in western Louisiana and adjacent east Texas, where it grows in wet pine savannas, seepage bogs, and roadside ditches. Also known as roughleaf or Sabine coneflower for its coarse, sandpapery leaves, it is a tall perennial with yellow-rayed, dark-coned flowerheads typical of the genus, blooming in mid-to-late summer and attracting a range of bees and butterflies. Because of its narrow native range and wetland habitat requirements it is uncommon in cultivation, but it is grown by regional native-plant specialists for bog gardens and rain gardens with consistently damp soil.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring in moist to average, organically rich soil in full sun to part shade; this variety naturally occurs in wet woods and bottomlands and tolerates more moisture than typical fulgida selections.

directions: Rudbeckia fulgida var. umbrosa occurs naturally in wet woods and bottomlands scattered from the Ozarks east to the Appalachians, distinguishing it from drier-site varieties by its fewer ray florets and broader, less deeply toothed leaves. It forms a rhizomatous, colony-forming clump that bears the classic golden-yellow, brown-coned daisy flowers from late summer into early fall, later than many other orange coneflower selections, providing valuable late-season nectar and pollen for bees and butterflies. It tolerates occasional standing water better than most Rudbeckia and is a good choice for the damper edges of a rain garden or pond margin.

planting.note: Scarify seed before direct sowing in spring in dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Florida wild indigo is adapted to sandhill and pine flatwoods conditions and dislikes rich, moist garden soil.

directions: Scarify seed (nick the hard coat with a file or soak in hot water overnight) before direct sowing in spring in dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Baptisia calycosa is a Florida endemic found in sandhills and pine flatwoods, where it forms a compact, rounded clump smaller than many of its wild indigo relatives. It bears the typical pea-like flowers of the genus in spring, followed by dark, hooked-beak seed pods around half an inch long. Being adapted to lean, excessively drained sandy soils, it is intolerant of heavy or poorly drained garden beds and, like other baptisias, forms a deep taproot that resents transplanting once established, so it should be sited permanently while young.

common_name: Ivory Towers False Indigo (Purple-Stemmed White False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, siting them permanently from the start since Baptisia forms a deep taproot and resents being moved or divided once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun and choose a permanent location, since Baptisia's deep taproot makes it a poor candidate for later transplanting or dividing. Bred at Plant Delights Nursery as part of the Towers series alongside 'Blue Towers', Ivory Towers is notable for the striking contrast between its terminal racemes of ivory-white flowers and the dark purple-tinged stems that hold them, in a narrow, upright, vase-shaped clump. Once established the plant is extremely drought tolerant, needs only an annual late-winter cutback, and its foliage serves as a larval host for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies.

common_name: Merlot Coneflower (Prairie Pillars Wine-Red Purple Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to rich soil in full sun; Merlot's stout, dark burgundy-black stems are strong enough to hold up its heavy bloom count without staking.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil with even moisture in full sun. Introduced by Terra Nova Nurseries as part of its Prairie Pillars collection, Merlot bears fragrant, red-purple flowers with bronzy-orange cones atop sturdy, dark wine-colored stems, so stout they rarely need staking even under a heavy bud load. It flowers from early summer into fall, and its petals reflex slightly downward as they age. It is drought tolerant once established and, like other purple coneflowers, attracts butterflies and hummingbirds and makes an excellent cut flower.

common_name: Fancy Frills Coneflower (Double Frilled Pink Purple Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Fancy Frills is an upright, vigorous double-flowered selection well suited to borders and cutting gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Introduced by Terra Nova Nurseries as a seedling from an open-pollinated cross with 'Ruby Giant', Fancy Frills produces large, fragrant, pink-purple flowers with distinctive frilled, doubled ray petals held out stiffly around a dark red-to-maroon central cone, giving it a shaggy, ornate look unlike single-flowered coneflowers. It blooms from midsummer into fall on an upright, vigorous clump, making an outstanding cut flower and drawing bees and butterflies. Deadhead to prolong bloom and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Green Eyes Coneflower (Magenta Pink Coneflower with Lime-Green Cone)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; sturdy, well-branched stems mean Green Eyes rarely needs staking.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Introduced by Terra Nova Nurseries from an open-pollinated cross with 'Ruby Giant', Green Eyes is a magenta-pink coneflower best known for its distinctive lime-green center cone on newly opened flowers, which gradually shifts to golden orange as blooms mature, giving each plant a two-toned effect over its bloom period. Overlapping, bright magenta-pink rays surround the cone on sturdy, well-branched stems that need no staking. It blooms from late spring to late summer, sometimes with sporadic rebloom into fall, and its mildly fragrant flowers are excellent for cutting and for attracting bees and butterflies.

common_name: Raspberry Tart Coneflower (Compact Deep Magenta Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this compact selection is well suited to borders and containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Raspberry Tart is a compact purple coneflower bearing small but extremely numerous, mildly fragrant, deeply saturated raspberry-magenta flowers with orange-bronze central cones, among the deepest-colored coneflower blooms available. It blooms from early summer into early fall, tolerates clay soil and drought once established, and resists deer browsing. Its compact habit makes it a good fit for borders, containers, and mass plantings, and it draws butterflies and other pollinators throughout its long bloom season.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant transplants in spring in well-drained, dry to average, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; wand blazing star is adapted to open woods and roadbanks from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia.

directions: Wand blazing star occurs naturally in open woods, barrens, clearings, and roadbanks from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia. Also known by the synonym Liatris regimontis, it produces slender wand-like spikes of rose-purple button flowers from midsummer into autumn, blooming later than many other blazing stars and providing a valuable late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and specialist native bees. It is one of the more common blazing stars in the Carolina piedmont and Blue Ridge foothills, tolerating lean, well-drained soils and thriving with minimal care once established.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
